analysis.one_liner: Creates government-seeded personal investment accounts alongside Social Security, with tax deductions for contributions.
analysis.headline: The bill never advanced past a subcommittee referral in May 1997, had no cosponsors, and died when the 105th Congress ended in January 1999.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have created a "personal Social Security investment account" for every child born on or after July 1, 1998, seeded with $1,000 taken from the sale of federal assets, and let anyone contribute up to $7,000 a year with a $2,000 income tax deduction. Retirement benefits would have been paid first out of these accounts, and the balances would have been converted to annuities bought from private insurance companies. It was never voted on in any committee or on the floor.
analysis.who_benefits: Higher-income workers come out best: the $2,000-a-year deduction is only worth anything to people who have $2,000 of spare cash to put in, and they can build the largest balances. Every child born after mid-1998 would get a $1,000 starter account invested in Thrift Savings Plan-style funds. The biggest structural winner is the financial industry: asset managers would run the fixed-income funds, and life insurers would sell the annuities that every retiring account holder would be required to purchase with their balance.

how_it_helps.text: Every child born on or after July 1, 1998 would automatically receive a $1,000 personal investment account, financed from federal asset sales and invested in Thrift Savings Plan-style options including a government securities fund, a fixed income fund, and a stock index fund.
Workers could contribute up to $7,000 a year to their account and deduct up to $2,000 of contributions from taxable income even without itemizing.
Retirees could choose how to draw the money: an annuity, deferred payments, a transfer to another retirement plan, or a lump sum if the balance is small, with the balance payable on death to heirs.

The bill includes spousal protections: a joint-and-survivor annuity is the default for married account holders, a spouse must consent to certain elections, and divorce decrees and child support or child-abuse judgments can reach the account.
The asset management industry would gain a new stream of publicly seeded accounts to manage, with fixed-income funds run by 'qualified professional asset managers' selected under the bill.

Life insurers and other annuity sellers would gain a captive market: the Executive Director must spend each retiree's balance buying an annuity contract from an entity that sells annuities in the normal course of business.

analysis.who_pays: The Treasury pays first: $1,000 for every newborn's account, funded by diverting proceeds from federal asset sales away from the general fund, plus the lost revenue from the up-to-$2,000-per-person deduction. If asset sales fall short, the President must recommend more federal asset sales under a fast-track procedure. Low-income workers get the least out of the deal because they cannot afford contributions to claim the deduction, and anyone choosing the stock or bond fund signs away any government guarantee on the return.
analysis.who_pays_short: Treasury, via asset sales and tax breaks

drawbacks.text: Account holders who pick the fixed income or stock index funds must sign an acknowledgment that the investment is at their own risk, with no government protection against loss and no guaranteed return.
The $2,000 tax deduction is worth most to households that can already afford to save $2,000 a year; workers living paycheck to paycheck get little from it.

The funding mechanism depends on selling federal assets, and if receipts are insufficient the President is required to recommend additional federal asset sales, considered under an expedited procedure that blocks amendments and limits debate.

The accounts would do nothing for anyone born before July 1998 and nothing to address Social Security's long-run finances, since the bill layers new costs on top of the existing benefit system rather than restructuring it.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill offers a modest, real benefit — a $1,000 head start for every newborn and a new tax-preferred savings channel — but the costs arrive long before the benefits: the Treasury funds the seeds and the deductions up front, while the accounts only pay out decades later to people born after 1998. The design channels the money through private fund managers and mandatory annuity purchases, so a large share of the value flows to the financial industry, and the returns for anyone in the market funds carry no guarantee. It also leaves Social Security's underlying finances untouched.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to a House Ways and Means subcommittee in May 1997 and never heard from again — no committee vote, no floor vote, and not a single cosponsor.

narrative.text: Rep. Thomas Petri introduced the bill on May 14, 1997; it was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee and, in addition, to the Rules Committee.
On May 29, 1997, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Social Security, which took no further action on it.
The bill attracted no cosponsors over its entire life.
No markup, committee vote, or floor vote ever occurred, and the bill expired when the 105th Congress ended on January 3, 1999.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Nothing changed: traditional Social Security continued as before, and the fund management and insurance industries did not get the new publicly seeded accounts. Taxpayers avoided the cost of the newborn accounts and the new deduction.

for.name: Rep. Thomas E. Petri
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and was its sole sponsor

against.name: House Ways and Means Subcommittee on Social Security
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on May 29, 1997 and never reported the bill or held a hearing or vote on it

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: Never considered or reported the bill during the entire Congress

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken on the bill; it had a single Republican sponsor, zero cosponsors of either party, and died in committee without any recorded support or opposition.

industries.note: The bill would route all account balances through a small set of government-securities, fixed-income, and stock-index funds, with fixed-income funds run by professional asset managers chosen under the bill. Account holders could share in market returns, but management is a new, essentially guaranteed business built on public seed money and up to $7,000 per person in annual contributions.

Every account holder's balance would have to be spent buying an annuity from a private annuity-selling entity when the account holder retires, creating a captive stream of customers. Retirees would get guaranteed income, but at annuity prices and terms set in a mandated purchase.
